blocks.md:
A **trait** names a set of methods that types can provide. It is Rust's way to say "any type that can do *this*". Other languages call it an interface. Traits answer the question left open in the last lesson: what does `T: PartialOrd` mean? It means "`T` implements the trait `PartialOrd`", so values of `T` can be compared.

*The Rust Programming Language* builds an aggregator that shows summaries of news articles and social media posts. Both should be able to `summarize()` themselves, so that behavior becomes a trait:

blocks.output:
1 new post: horse_ebooks: of course, as you probably already know, people
New article: Penguins win the Stanley Cup Championship!, by Iceburgh (Pittsburgh, PA, USA)
blocks.explain: The trait declares the method signature, ending in `;`. Each `impl Summary for Type` block provides the body for that type. To call a trait method, the trait must be in scope: other crates would write `use aggregator::Summary;`.

blocks.title: The orphan rule
blocks.md: You can implement a trait for a type only if **the trait or the type is local** to your crate. You may implement your `Summary` for `Vec<T>`, and the standard `Display` for your `SocialPost`, but not `Display` for `Vec<T>`: both belong to the standard library. This rule (part of *coherence*) guarantees that two crates can never provide conflicting implementations.

blocks.title: Default implementations
blocks.md: A trait can give a method a **default body**. Implementors get it for free and may override it. Default methods may call other methods of the trait, even ones without a default, so a type can implement one small method and receive a lot of behavior:

`fn f<T, U>(t: &T, u: &U) where T: Display + Clone, U: Clone + Debug`

blocks.output:
temperature: 21.5 is above the default
count: 0 is not above the default
blocks.explain: The `where` clause moves bounds after the signature, so the function name, parameters and return type stay readable. `U::default()` calls a trait method that has no `self`: it is called on the type.

blocks.title: Returning impl Trait
blocks.md: `-> impl Summary` says "this function returns some type that implements `Summary`" without naming it. It shines with closures and iterators (chapter 13), whose types are long or cannot be written at all. One restriction: the function must return a **single** concrete type. Returning a `NewsArticle` in one branch and a `SocialPost` in another does not compile; chapter 18's trait objects (`Box<dyn Summary>`) handle that case.

blocks.explain: The real return type is `Filter<RangeInclusive<u32>, {closure}>`, which you cannot name because closures have anonymous types. `impl Iterator<Item = u32>` hides it.

blocks.title: Conditional and blanket implementations
Associated types
blocks.md: Some traits need a type that each implementor chooses. `Iterator` is the main example: each iterator yields a different kind of item. The trait declares an **associated type** with `type Item;`, and each implementation sets it:

blocks.explain: Implementing only `next` gives `Countdown` every other iterator method, such as `sum`, `map` and `filter`, through default methods. *Programming Rust* contrasts associated types with generic traits: a type has one `Iterator` implementation (one `Item`), but may implement `Add<i32>` and `Add<f64>` separately.

blocks.title: Your own trait
blocks.md: Define a trait `Area` with a method `fn area(&self) -> f64` and a default method `fn describe(&self) -> String` that returns `"area = <area>"` with two decimals. Implement `Area` for `Circle` and `Rect`, then make `total_area` work for any slice of one shape type.
hints: `trait Area { fn area(&self) -> f64; fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("area = {:.2}", self.area()) } }`
`fn total_area<T: Area>(shapes: &[T]) -> f64` loops and adds `s.area()`.

blocks.title: A trait-based scoreboard
blocks.goal: Define a trait with required and default methods, implement it for several types, and write generic functions with bounds and impl Trait.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub trait Scored { fn points(&self) -> u32; fn name(&self) -> String; fn label(&self) -> String }` where `label` has a **default** body returning `"<name>: <points> pts"`.
- Implement `Scored` for `pub struct Player { pub name: String, pub points: u32 }` (uses the default label).
- Implement it for `pub struct Team { pub name: String, pub members: Vec<Player> }`: points are the sum of the members' points; **override** `label` to return `"Team <name>: <points> pts (<n> members)"`.
- `pub fn best<T: Scored>(items: &[T]) -> Option<&T>`: the item with the most points (the first on a tie), `None` if empty.
- `pub fn report(item: &impl Scored) -> String`: `"[" + label + "]"`.
hints: `fn label(&self) -> String { format!("{}: {} pts", self.name(), self.points()) }` inside the trait.
Team points: `self.members.iter().map(|p| p.points).sum()` or a loop.
In `best`, compare with `>` (strictly) so the first of equal items wins.
blocks.solution_explain: `Player` implements only the two required methods and inherits `label`; `Team` overrides it. `best` is generic, so one function handles slices of players and slices of teams. `report` uses `impl Scored`, the short form of the same idea.

questions.q: Which implementation does the orphan rule forbid in your crate?
questions.explanation: Both `Display` and `Vec` are foreign; at least one must be local.

questions.q: What is the difference between `fn f(a: &impl T, b: &impl T)` and `fn f<X: T>(a: &X, b: &X)`?
options: In the second, a and b must be the same type
questions.explanation: A named parameter ties both arguments to one type.

questions.q: Why can you call `.to_string()` on an `i32`?
options: A blanket `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`
questions.explanation: Anything that implements Display gets ToString.

questions.q: A function returns `impl Summary`. What is not allowed?
options: Returning a NewsArticle in one branch and a SocialPost in another
questions.explanation: It must be a single concrete type.

questions.q: A default method in a trait may call another trait method that has no default body.
questions.explanation: Implementors must provide that method, so the call is always valid.

questions.q: In `impl Iterator for Countdown`, what does `type Item = u32;` set?
options: The associated type: the type of items the iterator yields

points: A trait declares methods; `impl Trait for Type` provides them.
Default methods give behavior for free and can be overridden.
The orphan rule: the trait or the type must be local to your crate.
Use `impl Trait`, `<T: Trait>`, `+` and `where` to accept any type with the behavior.
`-> impl Trait` returns one unnamed concrete type.
Blanket impls (`impl<T: Display> ToString for T`) and associated types (`type Item`) are how the standard library is built.

terms.def: A named set of methods that types can implement, used to define shared behavior and to bound generics.
A requirement that a type parameter implements a trait, like T: Display.
You may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate.
An implementation of a trait for every type that meets a bound, like impl<T: Display> ToString for T.
A type declared inside a trait (type Item;) that each implementation chooses.
A place after a signature to list trait bounds, for readability.
